prime.problem: Your training step works but is slow: about 1000 ms per step even on an A100, and you have 19,073 steps to run. Every number is a 32-bit float by default, and the GPU's fastest matmul paths are locked behind formats with fewer bits.
prime.fits: You have a correct training loop that prints ms per step (the overfit card). This is the first card of "make it fast": it changes how numbers are stored and multiplied, not what the model computes.
expect: fp32, TF32, fp16 and bf16 (exponent vs mantissa bits)
gradient scalers (and why bf16 skips them)
prime.goal: Explain why TF32 gave 3× instead of 8×, pick bf16 over fp16 with a reason, and add TF32 plus bf16 autocast to your loop, timed honestly with a synchronize.

attend: If TF32 matmuls are 8× faster on paper, which part of a 1000 ms step does that 8× not reach?
TF32 keeps 32 bits in memory but bf16 autocast stores 16. Why does that difference matter for a memory-bound step?
Which single design difference between fp16 and bf16 removes the need for a gradient scaler?
Why does Karpathy wrap only the forward pass and the loss in autocast, and keep the weights and optimizer in fp32?
On the M3, why can the same autocast line give 0.97× at T=256 but 1.41× at T=1024?

must: TF32 rounds only inside the tensor cores → tensors still sit in memory as 32-bit fp32 → the time spent moving numbers is unchanged → 1000 → 333 ms (3×), not the datasheet's 8×

bf16 keeps fp32's 8 exponent bits and cuts the mantissa to 7 → same range (tiny gradients like 1e-8 survive) but coarse steps (eps 7.8e-3) → no gradient scaler needed, yet small updates and long sums round away

autocast covers only the forward pass and loss → matmuls run in bf16 while the stored weights, gradients and AdamW stay fp32 → speed from the matmuls without losing lr × grad updates that bf16 would round to nothing

the GPU runs asynchronously → time.time() right after step() measures only the queueing → you need torch.cuda.synchronize() / torch.mps.synchronize() before reading the clock, or every speedup you measure is fiction
elevated: build-nanogpt sets device_type = "cpu" for anything that isn't CUDA → on MPS tensors that autocast does nothing (logits stay fp32) → on a Mac the script silently trains in fp32 unless you pass 'mps'
fp16 has only 5 exponent bits → 70000 becomes inf and 1e-8 becomes 0 → fp16 training needs a GradScaler that scales the loss up before backward and back down after
reference: A100 non-sparse peaks: FP32 19.5, TF32 156, BF16 312 TFLOPS
bit layouts (sign/exponent/mantissa): fp32 1/8/23, TF32 1/8/10, fp16 1/5/10, bf16 1/8/7
torch.finfo(dtype) prints max, smallest normal and eps

compress.prompt: Card closed: draw the four bit layouts side by side, then write 3–4 sentences explaining why the A100 step went 1000 → 333 → 300 ms and not 1000 → 125 → 63 ms.
checklist: exponent bits set the range, mantissa bits set the precision
TF32 is fp32 in memory, rounded only inside the matmul unit
the step is partly memory-bound, so faster arithmetic alone gives ~3×
bf16 halves the bytes of the tensors autocast produces, but most of the win was already taken
bf16 has fp32's range, so no gradient scaler; fp16 does need one
weights and optimizer stay fp32 so small updates survive

retrieve.q: Explain the difference between range and precision in a float format, and say which one fp16 lacks and which one bf16 lacks.
answer: range: how big or small a number can be, set by the exponent bits
precision: how finely values are spaced, set by the mantissa bits (eps)
fp16 lacks range (5 exponent bits, max 65,504)
bf16 lacks precision (7 mantissa bits, eps 7.8e-3)

retrieve.q: Walk through one training step with bf16 autocast: which tensors are bf16, which stay fp32, and where does the gradient of lm_head.weight end up?
answer: inside autocast, matmuls take bf16 copies of the fp32 weights and activations
softmax, LayerNorm and the loss may stay fp32
the logits come out bf16
backward() runs outside the block; gradients flow back to the fp32 weights and land in fp32 .grad
AdamW updates the fp32 weights

retrieve.q: The datasheet promised 8× from TF32 and 16× from bf16, and the step got 3.0× and 3.3×. Using the toy Amdahl model, what share of the fp32 step must have been tensor-core arithmetic, and what should you attack next?
answer: so about 240 ms per step is memory traffic, elementwise ops and overhead
more arithmetic speed can't help that part
next: cut memory round trips and Python overhead (kernel fusion, torch.compile)

retrieve.q: Your teammate calls model.bfloat16() to save memory and training stalls. Give two concrete numeric reasons, and the fix.
answer: an update of 3e-4 to a weight of 1.0 rounds back to 1.0 in bf16
adding 0.01 a thousand times in bf16 stalls at 4.0
fix: keep the weights and optimizer fp32 and use autocast for the forward only

compare.q: Both this card and torch.compile / flash attention make the step faster. What is each one actually shrinking, and why does compile's 300 → 130 ms beat bf16's 333 → 300 ms?
answer: precision shrinks the cost of arithmetic (and, with bf16, the bytes per number)
fusion shrinks the number of round trips to GPU memory and the Python overhead
after TF32, the step is mostly memory-bound, so cutting trips pays more than cutting bits
precision can hurt accuracy if overdone; fusion gives the same loss to 6 decimals

compare.q: Padding the vocabulary to 50,304 and switching to bf16 both target the GPU's matmul units. What does each change, and why can either one show no gain on the M3?
answer: bf16 changes the number format so the fast tensor-core path can be used
padding changes the shape so the matmul tiles evenly
both depend on NVIDIA hardware details (tensor cores, tile sizes)
on MPS the measured effects are within noise: bf16 0.97–1.06× at T=256, padding 0.98–1.07×

predict.q: The next card adds torch.compile and changes no precision at all, yet takes the A100 step from 300 ms to about 130 ms. Before reading it: where must those ~170 ms have been going, given what bf16 could and couldn't fix?
predict.answer: Into memory traffic and overhead, not arithmetic. bf16 already had the fast matmuls and only saved 33 ms, so most of the remaining 300 ms is reading and writing tensors between GPU memory and the chip (every elementwise op like GELU or the residual add is a separate round trip) plus the Python interpreter launching each kernel. torch.compile fuses those ops into fewer kernels, which cuts the round trips.

apply.task: In your scratch folder, fill a (1000,) tensor with 0.01 in bf16. Add its elements one at a time into a bf16 accumulator and print the step at which the sum stops changing. Then compare with x.sum() on the same bf16 tensor and with x.float().sum(). Before running, use eps = 2−7 to predict the value where it stalls.
apply.done: The loop stalls at 4.0 after 350 additions (at 4.0 the gap between bf16 numbers is 4 × 2−7 = 0.03125, and 0.01 is less than half of it). x.sum() prints 10.0 and x.float().sum() prints 10.009765625, because torch accumulates internally in fp32 and 0.01 is stored as 0.010009765625.
apply.hint: Stop when acc + x[i] == acc. The spacing between bf16 numbers in [2k, 2k+1) is 2k × 2−7.
